newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa tumbles again, down 9 pct in three days.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa tumbles again, down 9 pct in three days.

text.p: CSCE cocoa fell sharply for the third straight day on Thursday, as speculators abandoned long positions in the belief that the market's month-long rally had come to an end.
September futures slid $52, to end at $1,562, amid heavy selling on the part of commodity funds.
The market tumbled from the opening bell, falling $89 a tonne in New York to a three-week low of $1,525. Scale-down trade buying helped the market to take back nearly half the losses by the close.

New York cocoa prices have declined by nearly nine percent in the past three days. Although there has been relatively little in the way of crop news during that time, analysts said a growing consensus that next season's West African harvest would fare better than originally thought set the stage for the downturn.
"I think the market basically came to its senses in the last couple of days," said Steve Platt, senior analyst with Dean Witter in Chicago.
"The market recognizes that the (1997/98) Ivory Coast crop is not experiencing any problems and could well come out where it was this year."

Technical factors also played a key role. On Wednesday, the benchmark September contract was unable to punch through a contract high of $1,737 set on June 24. The chart failure signaled to speculators the rally had lost its steam, said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka.

"That was a sign for a lot of speculators that they had better get out while the getting was good," he said. "People liquidate positions when the feel the market has gnoe up too quickly," he added, noting that the bulk of the recent rally occurred in just five sessions.

Traders also cited waning concerns about El Nino, a disruptive weather pattern that researchers have said could play havoc with global weather over the next 18 months. El Nino poses a particular threat to Indonesia, the world's third-biggest cocoa producer after Ivory Coast and Ghana.

The initial news about El Nino touched off cocoa's rapid rise to nine-year highs last month. But buyers later backed off after they realized El Nino posed little immediate threat to the key West African growing region.
"Sometimes the market gets way ahead of itself and that probably was the case in cocoa. El Nino won't take affect until later," Spilka said.
Traders and analysts also noted that cocoa's sharp upturn had come at the same time a sizzling rally in the coffee market began to falter.
A supply crunch in consuming nations briefly took world coffee prices to 20-year highs this spring, but that market has since pulled back substantially as the supply outlook has improved.

"The overreaction (in cocoa) could be traced to an influx of speculative interest, out of coffee and into cocoa, trying to build the case that it was a similiar situation, which it wasn't," said Dean Witter's Platt.

The CFTC is due to release its next Commitment of Traders data on Monday, July 7. But traders said since the figures will only reflect positions held through July 1, before the latest sell-off, the market is likely to pay them little heed.
Technically, the market could draw some support from September's settlement above $1,555. Next resistance would appear at $1,580, followed by $1,600. Support was seen at $1,514, a low from mid-June.
The CSCE will be closed on Friday, July 4, for Independence Day.
